dossier.public_summary: The 0.65-day dip sits exactly on the star's 0.651-day spot rotation and the out-of-eclipse light swings are nearly as large as the dip itself. The depth changes by about a third between sectors within the same data product as starspots evolve, and the transit density mismatch points to a pattern in the star's surface rather than an object transiting it. Difference imaging confirms the signal is on the target with no nearby star that could mimic it.

reasons.why: Signal period is exactly equal to the star's spot period, measured independently in every sector with amplitudes 46208 to 41590 ppm. A true transit would not match the rotation period this precisely.

Out-of-eclipse variability at the same period is almost as large as the 19320 ppm dip (ratio 1.18) with very high chi2, consistent with spot modulation folded at the rotation period rather than a planetary phase curve.

Depth changes significantly within the same detrending source, including a 37% drop from early sectors (~21357, 20950 ppm) to sectors 52-54 (14619, 14987, 14634 ppm), as expected when an evolving spot pattern changes apparent transit depth.

reasons.why: Even with the larger Gaia radius the transit density penalty is extreme and impact parameter is forced to zero, indicating the dip shape is more consistent with a finely-tuned spot dip on a small M dwarf than a planet transit.
